messages.content: I would like the average price of bitcoin at the end of each business week in 2023

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

message.content:
I’m sorry—I don’t currently have a way to pull live or archived financial‑market data into my responses. Because I can only make calls through the single “Open‑Meteo” helper you’ve been given, there’s no built‑in route for retrieving past Bitcoin prices. If you’d still like to calculate the weekly averages yourself, here’s what you’ll need: | Step | What to do | Where to find the data | |------|------------|------------------------| | **1** | Get daily close prices for BTC/USD for every day in 2023. | • CoinGecko public API (`https://api.coingecko.com/api/v3/coins/bitcoin/history`)
• CryptoCompare (`https://min-api.cryptocompare.com/data/histoday?fsym=BTC&tsym=USD&limit=365&toTs=`)
• Yahoo Finance CSV download (“Historical Data”) | | **2** | Identify the last trading day of each calendar week (Monday–Friday). For U.S. markets, weekends aren’t counted as business days. | Use a simple script or spreadsheet formula to pick Friday’s close for weeks where a Friday exists; for holidays skip accordingly. | | **3** | Compute the mean of the five daily closes within each week. | In Excel: `AVERAGE(B2:B6)` (assuming B2–B6 hold Monday–Friday closes); in Python pandas: `df.resample('W-FRI', label='right').mean()` after setting the index to dates. | Once you have the list of weekly averages, you can plot them or export them to whatever format suits your needs. --- ### Quick example in Python/pandas ```python import pandas as pd import yfinance as yf # pip install yfinance btc_hist = yf.download("BTC-USD", start="2023-01-01", end="2024-01-01") weekly_avg = btc_hist['Close'].resample('W-FRI').mean() print(weekly_avg) ``` This pulls the full year of daily close prices from Yahoo Finance, resamples to Fridays (the typical “end of business week”), and returns the weekly averages. Feel free to let me know if you run into trouble pulling the raw data—happy to help troubleshoot the code!
